title: Mountains, Waters and Sesshin, Part 4
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett reflects on how their experiences with various ceremonies and encounters have taught them the importance of being present and open-minded in their spiritual practice. They've learned to appreciate the value of silence, trust, and letting go of seeking validation from others, rather than trying to control or understand everything. This approach has helped them cultivate a sense of warmth, presence, and interconnectedness with all beings, including those who may be different from themselves.

sentences.text: Good morning everybody.
Sorry to keep you waiting.
I imagined I was learning another little lesson from my teacher, who was not often, but not unusually, late for talks.
I was just thinking, I had a "what would Norman do" moment.
I noticed that I was going to be late, and I thought, I don't think he would rush.
I don't think he would dawdle either.
I'd better get up and go to the zendo.
I just walked across the lawn.
For a while there were people still walking down there, and then at some point there weren't.
At some point I got here, and here you are.
It's kind of like that.
I forgot a few things, nothing too important.
Well, it seems like it's Friday, day seven.
At last, suddenly: oh yes, oh no, sorry, what day was that again?
That might be the best response.
Really?
Oh, okay.
I was just thinking about things that Norman didn't do.
What do we learn from that?
There's a pretty common trope in Dharma talks at sesshin to walk through the days.
To say to the group, maybe during the talk, or maybe in the evening as we're about to go to bed, "Well, it's day three.
We're closing our energy.
We're getting concentrated.
We're focusing in.
Well, it's day such-and-so."
Giving a little bit of coaching.
It's not the worst idea.
We are doing something kind of unusual, and even those of us who have done it before, it's not like what we are usually doing.
But Norman never did that, actually, and I don't know if he ever mentioned more than a word or two about how to actually practice sesshin.
He would have a topic in the Dharma that he was interested in exploring, and explore it with us.
We'd appreciate that.
Very few, if any, that I can remember, little tips about Zazen, or pacing yourself, or taking care of yourself at sesshin.
And he certainly talked to people about this individually.
He would bring it up.
It's not like he's saying "buck up, buttercup."
He would give suggestions, and not in the talks.
I don't know if he consciously thought about this, but maybe it's just another example of him somehow feeling deeply: these are strong, wise, self-reliant people.
They'll find their way.
They'll be okay.
I don't need to be the coach.
And then, when he started inviting me to give the first talk, I think something in me said, oh good, now somebody can be the coach.
Goodness gracious, this is our thing.
We should talk about this.
What are we doing here?
It'd be lovely if we're all just peaceably observing the Dharma, but we're struggling.
How do we do this?
So hopefully I didn't get too carried away, but I would try to give some suggestions that I thought would be helpful.
And actually, Norman giving me the first talk wasn't just trusting me and honoring that he didn't have to give all the talks anymore.
It was mostly practical.

Norman often somehow had one reason or another that he couldn't come to the first day or so of this sesshin, even though I was very careful every year to give him the dates right away and double check that he had them.
But somehow, in the intervening year, some important poetry event would come along.
For one day, sit, he wanted to lead in the Bay Area.
It hadn't occurred to him to get somebody to sub for him, even though he had many capable teachers down there.
It happened to be on the same first Saturday.
What do you know?
Sometimes, of course, very understandable things seem to be at the funeral for his teacher.
I think that year he missed a couple of days.
It was on a Sunday afternoon or something.
Some I had trouble deciding whether they were justified or not, like his granddaughter's elementary school graduation.
Yes, I said elementary school.
Kathy was here too, so she proceeded to educate me about how vitally important it is to have a good elementary school graduation to the future of New York school students.
Like your fate is kind of cast at age 10 in the Big Apple, and you need all the support you can get.
Definitely need your grandparents.
But of course, this was also just more teaching on trust, even if I sometimes didn't appreciate it.
One of these messages actually came while we were in Japan.
I don't know if I told anybody on the trip, but we were having one of the flexible days we had in Kyoto.
And Raizelah and I, I can picture the temple that I remember, Nansenji maybe, one of the big Rinzai temples.
I checked my phone and there was an email from Norman saying, oh, by the way, I'll be there late.
I've got this other thing I've got to do.
So I sat there writing an argument back: oh, no, no, no, you need to come to sesshin.
I think there was one time I did convince him and he did come.
But it was one out of 20 or something.
So anyway, he didn't talk a lot about how to practice sesshin while at sesshin.
I guess he just trusted that we were figuring it out.
And I'm sure that we are.
Being a little obsessed with silence, I can't resist mentioning that at the moment, but I'll be brief.
It's easy to feel pretty comfortable towards the end sometimes.
You're sitting on the bench next to some really nice person and you both have your coffee.
It's so natural to say, oh, isn't this great?
Where are you from again?

So one good thing to remind yourself of, and it's not just about following rules or because some authority figure told you this is better, is that it's super helpful and super fun to tune in to the positive side of each of these guidelines.
To ask yourself, what does deep silence bring me in this moment if I didn't say, "Isn't this nice?"

In my own experience, you see for yourself, but my own experience is that to sit in deep, companionable silence with somebody, totally content, totally trusting that the other and yourself don't need to say anything, is so beautiful.
Don't you think?
It's so lovely.
And it pretty much takes this huge apparatus and a week of sitting to make that actually possible.
Otherwise, right, we feel self-conscious.
The silence has dragged on too long.
Ah, what's her name again?
Right?
What did they tell me about there?
I should have told you.
Just to be together, to feel the energy of two human bodies living and breathing, that you're feeling the sun together, enjoying the scenery together.
That's so beautiful.
So you think about it that way, and you're like, well, I don't want to spoil this beautiful moment with chit chat.
There's plenty of chit chat in the world.
Let's just be together quietly.
If you're lucky, the other person comes to the same conclusion and you can do it together.
And if they say hi, of course, we're polite.
Yeah, it is beautiful.
So let's go back once again.
Is the sound okay?
It's a little bit lower than I've had it.
Okay, I think it's kind of falling down.
Is that better?
Actually, I forgot my sound check.
Okay, yeah, you were straining to hear, you didn't hear any of that.
Okay, probably just as well.
Now here's my actual talk.
Let's go back to June of 1993, our first ever retreat.
I've talked a lot about the history of this retreat, but there's one thread running throughout it from the beginning.
Florence Caplow, of course, was here.
She and I were the main co-conspirators running the Bellingham Zen Practice Group in the first few years.
Maybe you've met Florence or know her name from the wonderful book she co-wrote called The Hidden Lamp, Zen Stories Through Two Centuries.
So, of course, she was here.
And Florence loved to sit.
I'll never forget this.
One time early on she told me that on the weekend, we were all working full-time and all this, but on the weekend she would have to bargain with herself.
So she'd get her chores done and not just sit all day.
I remember this, I'm pretty sure she said this: she'd say to herself, "If you get the vacuuming done, then you can sit for a couple of hours."
So it was amazing to me.
I deeply appreciate sitting, but it does not call to me in that way, like, yeah, I can't wait.
I've got some time off, I'm going to sit till they make me do something.
So Florence and I had a fuller schedule, but she wanted to sit more after the schedule.
And she was sitting up late one night here in this room at our first sesshin.
And she had a shocking and horrific vision experience.

We use the word vision for this kind of thing, but I don't know how visual it was exactly, if she saw things in a visual way, or if it was more of a sudden bunch of feelings or more somatic: constriction, tension, heat.
But she had some kind of really occult experience.
An experience of pain, horror, and suffering.
She was sitting here breathing and this thing overtook her.
I think after she got up and left and walked for a while, it faded again.
I remember I doubt she slept very much that night.
So she went to see Norman in the morning, and they intuited together that maybe this was an experience to do with restless spirits here at this place, because it was our first time practicing here.
And Florence had some street cred around indigenous peoples.
She had recently married a guy who's a lawyer, he might still be, a lawyer for the Lummi tribe, really connected to the tribe.
And their wedding was on the Lummi Nation's sacred lands at Madrone Point on Orcas Island, where normally non-tribal members never get to go.
The officiant and most of the guests were tribal members.
They took us out there on a boat from Bellingham.
It was quite an experience for me.
I was kind of newish in town.
I went, wow, this is interesting.
I remember the wedding was really long.
Everyone who spoke was, in my view, really long-winded.
But most of the people in the audience, I was interested to see, didn't feel obligated to sit there and listen to it all.
They'd get up, wander outside, chat a little bit, wander back in, and then nudge each other at different bits.
It was just a little different culture than I was used to.
So Florence had some feeling of that world, at least as it expresses now.
And this was long before there was anything posted on the walls in the dining room, so we really didn't know much about the Samish Nation.
And they weren't recognized by the federal government.
In the treaties of the 1860s, they got left out somehow.
Or 1880s, I guess it was.
So we were kind of ignorant of where we were going.
We knew it was called Samish Island.
If we'd thought about it, we probably would have assumed that was a native name, like half the names around here, hardly pronounced.
But we didn't know much.
There's one thing on the walls that is back from those days.
It's a little frame with some faded newspaper clippings in it.
Not much information.
But Florence and Norman figured this was something to do with the people who had been here.
So Norman said we should do a spirit-settling ceremony.
If you've ever been to a hungry ghost ceremony, segaki or sejiki, you know the kind of thing we're talking about.
But if you don't, I'll just remind you.
It's much more, dark isn't the right word, but it kind of is.
Esoteric, going deep.
Most of the chanting is mantras and Dharanis.
The officiants are invited to really try to express something of what you might call the other world.
Because the Zen Buddhist tradition, it turns out, isn't just meditation and a way to get enlightened, although that was the story that was important to the U.S.
It absolutely includes a deep root in esoteric ritual and understanding.
And we're constantly, in all the chants, talking about the six worlds and the three realms and this of that and that of this.
Stuff that you can't see.
You can't even really talk about.
That it's here.
The other Japanese Buddhisms actually specialize in this a little more, with a big ritual repertoire.
Mudras and mantras.
Interesting uses of malas.
When we went to Japan we also got to meet a great practitioner in that world.
At one point he came around and whacked us on the head with his mala while chanting something really fast that we didn't understand, to help wake us up.
We were able to talk about fire ceremonies, ceremonies done in the dark, ascetic practices.
Ways to bend conventional reality so we could see more clearly what's beyond what we thought we could see.
So we're doing something like that. [unclear: "We made Gather Together"].
It was a big community event.
We talked about it a lot each year.
We'd gather together all kinds of offerings and lay out a big table for an altar out in the field over there.
We'd do lots of chanting.
Norman was the doshi at first, of course.
He would really go into [unclear: "his god"].
Into his aura.
Express something of our reverence, our sadness, some of the stuff I was trying to say yesterday.
With the dial at 11.
I tried to keep it at 8 or 9.
Maybe only 7 or 8.
So that we can really reach these spirits.

Try to offer something that might help, and acknowledge that we know we're on their sacred grounds, and that we know that many of our family ancestors were involved in horrors here, even though we didn't know a lot about what those horrors were.
A couple of years in, Kate and Jeff McKenna joined the sangha.
They've been on Zoom but aren't on today, so I can talk about them more freely, maybe.
They could listen.
Anyway, Kate and Jeff McKenna joined the sangha.
And Jeff is a white guy from Texas, but he came up here for all kinds of reasons and was adopted into one of the tribes.
He has a tribal family, and has a pretty good sense, through his own conditioning for sure, but a good sense of native ways and rituals.
So he'd come and help us arrange the altar.
And he was really surprised.
Actually, I heard this from Jeff over and over again, in many different ways.
He was really surprised by how similar many of the rituals and forms and ways of holding the body are to things that he had seen at tribal events.
For instance, when we do prostrations and hold our hands like this, this is the universal gesture of gratitude and reverence in the Coast Salish people.
Just the same.
Just the same.
Jeff said what we were doing with this hungry ghost ceremony was like a ritual they call a burning.
Very similar, he said.
Done when there was a funeral, and other important occasions.
So I'm watching all this and feeling into all this, and of course being a good person, an eager helper, helping with all this, and trying to make sense of it.
Because I grew up really non-religious, the son of a physicist.
He'd actually go on to be a pretty prominent American physicist.
Living in the suburbs.
I did have a groovy grandmother.
That's my main inspiration for practice.
You come back with stories of healers in Brazil and stuff like that.
But for the most part I didn't know about this stuff.
In my teens I definitely had been loosened up a bit by my experiences out in nature, with psychedelics, starting to dabble in meditation.
But I didn't have any background on what the heck this was.
And I was absolutely quite allergic to new agey stuff.
I went to school in Santa Cruz, California, a bastion of hippie culture.
There was a crystal shop on every corner.
People were doing healing things of all kinds.
Pyramids were involved.
I thought it was bunk.
So that was a funny combination, I guess, of spiritually curious and narrow-minded skeptic, all bundled up together.
Feeling the "what the heck."
And here I was helping to call to the spirits.
Making offerings.
Apologizing for the pain.
Taking some responsibility for it.
Shouting into the wind.
Watching the tide.
Funny how things can go, huh?
After a while, after I ordained and Norman was by now like a full-time resident of his dokusan hut, he said, "Well, you leave that stuff."
I don't remember any training.
So I did.
I tried.
I was enthusiastic about everything, trying to do a good job.
And I started noticing something.
Every year, during or after or sometime in there, at these ceremonies, I felt this odd feeling that I never fairly felt before that I could remember.
A dense sort of feeling of warmth, centered in my gut.
It sounds pretentious to say a kind of presence, but that word did come.
What is this feeling?
It didn't feel painful or bad.
Maybe it was a good thing.
This is the spirits, whatever the heck that is.
And it would gradually fade as we walked back to the dining hall for dinner, like we did last night.
Then sesshin is crammed full, and this is one hour out of many and one week out of many in the year, and I'd forget all about it again, until it came right around.
I'm pretty sure I mentioned this feeling to Norman at some point, and I'm pretty sure he said something like, "Oh, that's interesting."
But I was also a little uncomfortable and embarrassed about it.
Am I making this up?
Am I trying to force myself to feel something?
Am I trying to be special or spiritual or a pseudo-shamanic practitioner?
So I felt a little conflicted too, I think.
But it kept coming back, the same feeling every year, and over the years it really felt like it was getting stronger.
In the meantime I, and we, started learning more about the history of what happened here, based mostly on examples of very similar places.
Not much is written, if anything, specifically about what happened to this village here.
But it must have been like the other ones.
That learning was intense for me, learning more about the degree of suffering, and that we are here because of it in many ways.
It was intensely embarrassing and a little shameful that I didn't know all this.
I didn't grow up in the West.
California Native people were squashed and sidelined a little earlier because of the gold rush and stuff.
Still, they were there.
I knew a little bit about Native people, but mostly at arm's length.
I had a few books.
I had met an important anthropologist one time and talked about it.
I remembered from school being taught something like: there were these diseases that the Europeans brought, but bad luck for the Natives, they didn't have any resistance to them.
Sort of like an unhappy accident.
Regrettable.
And then here I am, many years later, reading about smallpox.
It arrived at a particular moment on a boat in Victoria, British Columbia, in 1862.
By then Victoria had become a major trading hub, and Native people would come in their canoes from up and down the coast to trade with each other and with the white people.
So there were a lot of people around from the Indigenous communities when smallpox arrived.
And they all left with it, too.
They went back to their homes, and it spread so quickly.
Then I learned that this story about it being bad luck that they didn't have immunity was a half-truth at best.
You get pretty sick if you're a European person in the 1860s getting smallpox, but maybe you don't die.
The Native people all died, pretty much.
I read that the mortality was between 60 and 90 percent in each village.
I try to get my head around these numbers.
Picture a group of friends like this group, so what, 28 people here: four of us surviving?
Five?
And I was reminded that we absolutely had a vaccine.

Maybe you remember from high school biology the thing about cows, giving them a mild version of the whatever it was, and then they strangely survived, and you can take some blood from them and give it to another cow, and that cow strangely survives.
That was in the 1790s, long before contact.
I read there was at least one doctor who went to several villages on Vancouver Island administering vaccine, and as a result those peoples did much better.
But that was the exception, not the rule.
All this made me, and my Sangha colleagues, at least the ones who were learning about this and talking about this with me, get a little intense about it.
It's understandable.
A little messianic.
I was happy to have an excuse to use the word messianic, even though it's a strong word, actually.
People need to know about this, you know.
They may have thought they signed up for a Buddhist retreat, but it turns out they're at a teach-in on Native American studies, and we need to share this with them.
We weren't wrong, right?
But our energy was a little bit off.
So there were a couple of years where it must have been sometimes a little uncomfortable.
There were a couple of years where I think it was usually me.
It was probably always me, in the Zazen period after a work meeting that went on pretty long.
We've had the shortest work meetings in history.
Thank you, [unclear: "Jeri Kisama"].
We used to have longer work meetings, maybe even longer, because of all the things I wanted to say.
Sometimes I go on at length at the work meeting: we're going to appreciate the sacred ground and what happened here in genocide.
Great.
Enjoy your work for me.
And then we're going to do something about it too.
Please, after work, gather some things for our altar.
See if you can find things that would have been here before contact, so the spirits will recognize them.
Not dandelions, but Douglas fir cones.
I'm sure it was driven partly by guilt.
Why is it we get to be here now?
What have we colluded in?
It also made me reflect that the settlers were not all evil people or anything like that.
They were people just like us, just like me, trying to find a way to live.
Living in a slum in the east somewhere and being offered 80 acres of free land, which you do.
By the government, must be legit.
And when they got here, given the massive depopulation from disease and the reservation system that was starting up, it was: we'll just relocate you to this undesirable spot over here.
Oh, that actually was desirable.
We'll relocate you again.
That happened several times.
I was reading, actually, I didn't know this, that the Squamish tribe in Vancouver had a similar thing.
Did you know about this?
I guess it happened a little while ago.
They were given all the lands along False Creek, if you've been to Vancouver, which at that point the city of Vancouver didn't care about.
It was out in the sticks.
It's this long inlet called False Creek.
They could stay living there and expand their village, and their village was to become their reservation.
It was called something like Kitsilano.
Maybe you know the neighbourhood called Kitsilano now.
So eventually the white people said, "No, we want that land, you're out of here."
Then, not too many years ago, the tribe sued and said, "Those are our lands."
And they won.
They didn't give them back the whole neighbourhood of Kitsilano, full of single-family houses and retired people and stuff.
But there were ten acres of unused land not far away, because it had been like a railroad switching yard or something like that, and the railroad was defunct.
So the tribe got it, right on the edge of downtown Vancouver, not too far.
It's so encouraging just reading about this.
So what did they do?
They developed high-rise housing.
Thousands of units, enough for all of their tribe who might want to live in the Vancouver area, and a couple thousand more for rentals.
And they're making a lot of money as landlords.
Good for them.

The article listed some of the complaints from the neighbours, and one of them, boy, I hope this person is embarrassed now to be in the New York Times saying, "That's not actually indigenous housing."
Anyway.
So sometimes the tribes get a little back.
There's a similar thing with the Nisqually people in Tacoma, actually, too.
All of the Port of Tacoma actually belongs to them.
Anyway, that's not the usual thing.
The usual thing is like here.
They're gone.
And what can we as Zen students sitting here do about it?
How should we feel about it?
How should we practice with it?
So over a couple of years we got a little intense about it.
But it was still all third-hand knowledge.
Then in the spring of 2009 the Community of Christ organized a 50th anniversary event.
The campground was founded in 1959.
We were invited to come.
I led a meditation.
It turned out it was mostly church elders I taught meditation to.
That was cool.
But the amazing thing was that the Samish Nation also came.
They sent several elders and younger people supporting them.
They spoke about this place.
I don't remember a lot of what they said.

One of them was an elder named Rosie, and I actually had just heard that name a couple of months before, so that was really surprising. [unclear: "Our same"] Jeff McKenna had been to another event, and somehow I think it had to do with the Maiden of Deception Pass statue, which was made by a Samish carver, although that was carved quite a bit earlier.
I'm not sure.
But anyway, he's a very gregarious guy.
He has an inn.
So he was schmoozing.
He's a great schmoozer.
And he got to chatting with elders of the Samish Nation, this woman Rosie.
She listened a little while to who he is.
He talked about Red Cedar and stuff, and she said to him, "Oh, are you the ones that have been calling to us?"
And we had not called them on the phone.
We did not.
So that was powerful information to hear.
And here she is.
Here she is, at Samish.
I was way too shy to talk to her.
But I talked to another tribal member, a woman about my age, and shared with her about this ceremony.
I think the anniversary thing was in May or April, so it was not too long until we were going to be here.
That was good.
I told her, "We've been doing this ceremony for your people.
We'd love for you to be there.
We hope it will feel right.
And we want your input.
We'd be honoured if you came."
And she said yes, just right away.
She said, "I'll call you.
Let me check my schedule."
And then, yes.
She and her husband, who was from a plains tribe of some kind, I think, both came.
We did the whole thing.
They were so appreciative.
I saw tears in their eyes.
Like we did yesterday, after our outdoor ceremony, at the end we all filed back in to get our chant books back, to return to our sesshin space.
We did that, had the formal exit and continued to dinner.
This Samish woman, I'm embarrassed I didn't get her name, I forgot it, then stepped forward before we left and spoke to us in the Samish language, thanking us.
It might have only been a few minutes, but it felt like an eternity, that language ringing out in this room.
Maybe right about where the village longhouse was, where that language was always ringing out.
So then we felt like, okay, we're doing something.
Then the next year it all went a little off the rails.
We were gearing up for our big usual ceremony.
It might have been the very next year, so I maybe had some feeling of inspiration from this actual encounter with actual Samish people.
I was outside getting ready and feeling into the vibe, like I was doing yesterday, although I didn't realize you were already there.
Sorry you had to wait a while.
Jeff was by my side.
Maybe this other Zen priest from that little diaspora I was telling you about was by my side too.
He's into this kind of stuff.
And this year I felt that strong gut feeling right away.
Really strong.
Before we could even start the ceremony, I was looking out at where we had it set up, and I felt like this pull, like a string pulling out this feeling, pulling me to another part of the ground.
It's over closer to where they have now their compost and rubble pile.
But somehow I just knew that that's where we needed to be.
I just knew it.
And I heard a strange-sounding voice telling everybody we need to move over there, which didn't quite sound like me, but it was.
Everyone looked at me, I guess, and we moved.
They're good Zen students, in silence.
But I'm sure people were starting to wonder what's going on here.
The ceremony was very powerful, and that feeling was so strong.
As we walked to dinner it didn't start to fade like it always had.
If anything it felt stronger, like it was growing.
I don't really remember.
I'm trying to project back, but I think it must have been a wild mix of feelings in me.
Fear.
Maybe pride.
Lots of confusion.
What's going on here?
Am I being possessed?
What's happening?
Jeff and John took me under their wing when I went to tell them after dinner.
They'd been hovering.
They said, "Something's going on with Tim."
And they concocted some kind of ritual to help me clear this.
It involved water in a big bowl.
I don't know what it all was.
They were pretty clear about what they thought would be best.
Maybe it helped.
It was fading a little bit.
But then I suddenly felt really concerned for everybody else.
There are moments when you're really upset and you're halfway back to normal, and you think you're back to normal, and then you go and do something.
You know what I mean?
You're half possessed by your emotions, and so I'm half possessed by Samish spirits.
Zazen had already started, but I thought, I need to warn people.

So I went into the Zendo, and during the silence of Zazen, in my altered state, in what I thought was a very calm, reasonable, simple voice, I explained that if they had any weird feelings they should probably get them checked out.
Shamanic healers are standing by.
You may now return to your normal Zazen program.
This has been a message of the Emergency Spiritual Broadcasting Network.
So it was deep in sesshin and people were keeping the silence, and I did my thing and sat down and sat Zazen.
I think it was more or less calm enough that I could get to sleep eventually.
Pretty wired.
And unbeknownst to me, a delegation of the [unclear: "owners"] had all gone to see Norman and explained that Tim was now completely off the rails and needed an intervention.
You probably need to relieve him of his leadership responsibilities too.
I heard a little bit about this from a few of them, I think, because they were too embarrassed to ever tell me about this conversation.
I think some of them are here, so forgive me.
But I think Norman more or less said, "Hmm, sounds like Tim had a strong experience.
Let's let him get a good night's sleep.
And he is qualified to leave the sesshin, so it'll be okay."
He expressed his trust and sent them off to bed.
And I don't think anyone really talked to me during, you know, it's always a little party after, and people just didn't know how to bring this up.
Nobody talked to me.
Then a couple of days later the phone rang and it was Norman.
That's unusual, he didn't usually call me.
And he says Well, so probably we shouldn't do that ceremony anymore.
And he explained, he thought about this.
He explained, well, that might be important work for somebody to do.
But our main purpose is to offer a Zen sesshin.
So we don't want something else to disturb that too much.
I think he said a little disturbance is okay.
I somehow managed to suggest, I'm usually very compliant if anyone tells me I've been bad.
I'm like, "I'm so sorry."
But I kind of stayed in myself and said, "Well, yeah, I can see that.
But I suggest, well, maybe a simpler ceremony.
Can we try that?"
He said, "Yeah, yeah.
We could try that."
